title: Find the Town Judge
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning the trust list per candidate versus a single combined pass building two count arrays.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: In a town of n people labeled 1 to n, given a list of trust pairs [a, b] meaning person a trusts person b, find the town judge: the one person trusted by EVERYONE else but who trusts NO ONE. Return their label, or -1 if no such person exists.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","n, trust pairs"],["Output","The town judge's label, or -1"],["Key Insight","Track two counts per person: how many people they trust (must be exactly 0), and how many trust them (must be exactly n-1)"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 people"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"One person trusted by everyone, trusting no one\"","This is exactly a directed graph in/out-degree problem: the judge has in-degree n-1 and out-degree 0"]]}

blocks.text: Model trust as a directed edge from a to b. The town judge is exactly the person with OUT-DEGREE 0 (trusts no one) and IN-DEGREE n-1 (trusted by every other person). Tracking these two counts for every person in a single pass over the trust list directly identifies the judge, if one exists.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding a Universally Respected Referee Who Answers to No One
blocks.text: Picture a group where certain people vouch for others. The one person everyone else vouches for, but who vouches for no one themselves, would be a natural, universally trusted referee, identifiable by simply counting how many vouch for each person and how many each person vouches for.

blocks.caption: Track two counts per person: trusts (must be 0) and trusted-by (must be n-1)

blocks.text: Result: 2 (person 2 is trusted by person 1 and trusts no one).
Result: -1 (person 3 trusts person 1, so person 3 cannot be the judge, and no valid judge exists).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The judge must have OUT-DEGREE exactly 0 (trusts no one), since a true judge answers to nobody.

Observation 2: The judge must have IN-DEGREE exactly n-1 (trusted by every other one of the n-1 other people).

Observation 3: Both of these counts can be tracked simultaneously in a SINGLE pass over the trust list, incrementing an out-count for the truster and an in-count for the trustee on every pair.

Observation 4: After this single pass, checking every person for out-count 0 and in-count n-1 directly identifies the judge, if one exists; if no person satisfies both conditions, return -1.
This leads to a single pass building two count arrays (trusts given, trusts received), then a scan checking both conditions.
For each candidate person, scan the ENTIRE trust list twice: once to check they trust no one, and once to count how many people trust them.
Why the code is written this way

items: Scanning the trust list per candidate directly checks the definition for each person.
This repeats redundant full scans for every candidate, costing O(n times trust length); a single combined pass building both counts avoids all this repetition.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times trust.length).
Space: O(1) extra per candidate check.
Limitation: a single pass over trust, building both count arrays simultaneously, computes everything needed in one linear scan.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Initialize two arrays, trustCount and trustedByCount, both of size n+1, all zeros. For each pair [a, b] in trust, increment trustCount[a] (a trusts someone) and trustedByCount[b] (b is trusted by someone). After this single pass, scan every person from 1 to n; return the first one with trustCount equal to 0 AND trustedByCount equal to n-1. If none qualifies, return -1.
Use a single pass building two count arrays, then a single scan checking both conditions.

Building both count arrays in a single combined pass correctly captures every person's out-degree (trustCount, how many they trust) and in-degree (trustedByCount, how many trust them) simultaneously; the town judge, by definition, is the unique person with out-degree exactly 0 and in-degree exactly n-1, directly identified by a single final scan checking both conditions together.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n plus trust.length).
Space: O(n) for the two count arrays.

blocks.text: Find the Town Judge is a clean introduction to directed graph in-degree/out-degree reasoning, expressed in an approachable, non-graph-labeled way.

items: Forgetting the judge must have out-degree EXACTLY 0, not just a low trust count.
Off-by-one errors comparing trustedByCount against n instead of n-1 (the judge does not need to be trusted by themselves).

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "this is an in-degree/out-degree problem in disguise" demonstrates recognizing an underlying graph structure in an approachable problem framing.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "one entity trusted or referenced by everyone, referencing no one", think: track in-degree and out-degree per node, look for the (0, n-1) combination.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The per-candidate scanning approach costs O(n times trust.length); the single combined pass costs O(n plus trust.length), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: directed graph in-degree/out-degree tracking, in a single combined pass.
Core Idea: the judge has out-degree exactly 0 and in-degree exactly n-1.
Time: O(n times trust.length) for the brute force, O(n plus trust.length) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) extra per candidate for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: this is an in-degree/out-degree problem, just not labeled as a graph explicitly.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy graph-adjacent counting problem.
One line memory trick: out-degree 0, in-degree n-1.
